# Purine and pyrimidine-based bacterial cyclic dinucleotides egress the phagosome and activate the cytoplasmic innate immune sensor STING

**Authors:** Stephanie A. Ragland; Katherine E. Lindblad; Yao Li; Joon H. Choi; Daniel Okin; Joshua Q. Mao; Desmond Richmond-Buccola; Daniela R. Coronado; Madison R. Brown; Scott B. Snapper; Philip J. Kranzusch; Jonathan C. Kagan

## Abstract

Toll-like Receptors (TLRs) are considered general sensors of bacterial encounters. Here we examined whether other pattern recognition receptors are commonly activated during bacterial infection. TLR-independent interferon (IFN) responses were induced in macrophages in response to diverse bacterial encounters. Of the cytoplasmic receptor families examined, the cyclic dinucleotide (CDN) sensor STING was required for IFN responses to evolutionarily diverse bacteria. Various bacterial CDNs were present in murine tissues; these activated STING after bacteriolysis in phagolysosomes in a manner requiring two CDN transporters. Importantly, bacterial CDNs were increased in colonic biopsies from inflammatory bowel disease patients. Systemic delivery of dead, CDN-laden bacteria promoted anti-tumor immunity in mice. Detection of diverse CDNs, including pyrimidine-based CDNs, was an evolutionarily conserved feature of STING, with distinct binding modes for purine- and pyrimidine-based CDNs. Thus, a phagocytosis-CDN-STING connection places cytoplasmic sensing as a common outcome of host-bacteria interactions that set the immune tone of a tissue, with implications for host defense.

## Abstract

Innate immune recognition of bacteria is thought to center on cell surface or endosomal pattern recognition receptors such as the TLRs. Ragland et al. identify an intraphagosomal-cyclic dinucleotide (CDN)-host transporter-STING axis, wherein cytoplasmic STING acts as a common sensor of diverse bacteria, capable of detecting broad array of CDN species including pyrimidine-based CDNs.

## INTRODUCTION

Central to the functions of innate immune pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) is their ability to bind microbial molecules known as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). PAMPs in the extracellular and endosomal spaces are commonly detected by members of a single PRR family in mammalian cells, the Toll-like Receptors (TLRs)1. The cytoplasmic space, in contrast, harbors a spectrum of PRRs, including the RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), the nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat containing proteins (NLRs), AIM2-like receptors (ALRs), cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS), and stimulator of interferon genes (STING)2–4. Despite this diverse repertoire of PRRs, our understanding of how and when PAMPs cross the plasma or phagosomal membranes to access the cytosol is incomplete. The spectrum of PAMPs that can cross membranes to access cytoplasmic PRRs (and their mechanisms of transport) have largely been studied in the context of pathogenic bacteria that induce phagosomal membrane damage. As such, cytoplasmic PRRs are often framed as pathogen-specific receptors5,6. TLRs, in contrast, due to their relative ease of PAMP access in the extracellular and luminal endosomal environments where most bacteria are located, are considered the only PRR family that functions as a general sensor of bacterial encounters.

Despite this prevailing view, cytoplasmic PRRs can have a role in non-pathogen encounters, including Escherichia coli, Mycobacterium smegmatis, and Listeria innocua7–9. Chemically-synthesized and/or pure PAMPs can be translocated from the extracellular space or endosomal lumen to the cytosol. For example, peptidoglycan fragments that stimulate the NLRs NOD1 and NOD2 are endocytosed and then translocated into the cytosol by one of several transport proteins10–12. Cyclic dinucleotides (CDNs) that stimulate STING are also translocated across the plasma membrane into the cytosol by several transporters13–17. However, these transporters have been studied primarily in the context of pure PAMPs. We therefore have limited knowledge for their role in cellular encounters with actual microorganisms.

In this study, we report that STING is activated after intraphagosomal bacteriolysis by a wide spectrum of CDNs produced by evolutionarily diverse bacteria. This diversity of CDN structures was detected in the tissues of mice and in clinical samples isolated from healthy humans and those with inflammatory bowel disease. Two CDN transporters, SLC46A2 and LRRC8A15–17, supported STING activation by intraphagosomal bacteria producing diverse CDN chemical structures. Our findings from in vitro infections of macrophages enabled the use of dead, CDN-laden bacteria as a platform to drive anti-tumor activity in two cancer models. Furthermore, CDNs that contain pyrimidine bases were potent STING agonists. X-ray crystallography defined mechanisms by which pyrimidine- and purine-based CDNs differentially bind to this PRR. These findings establish STING as a versatile sensor that underlies commonplace host-bacteria interactions.

## Results

### Evolutionarily diverse bacteria stimulate TLR-independent interferon (IFN) responses in macrophages.

To identify common PRR activities in macrophages, we studied evolutionarily diverse bacteria consisting of 13 species of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, most of which associate with humans without causing disease (Figure 1A and Table S1)18–29. We performed infections of wild-type (WT) primary murine bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and measured secretion of the immunomodulatory proteins TNFα, interferon β (IFNβ), and IP-10. All bacteria induced the secretion of these factors within 24 hours (Figure 1B). Production of IFNβ and IP-10, which are constituents of an IFN response, was stimulated by gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria generally within 4 and 24 hours, respectively. IFNβ secretion corresponded with the phosphorylation of the IFN-responsive transcription factor STAT1 (STAT1 Y701 phosphorylation, “pSTAT1”) and the production of the IFN stimulated gene (ISG) product viperin (Figures S1A–D). Injection into the mouse peritoneum with gram-positive non-pathogens also resulted in increased pSTAT1 and viperin abundance, compared to PBS controls (Figure 1C).

We performed similar experiments in immortalized BMDMs (iBMDMs) and observed IFN response kinetics and magnitudes to all bacteria that was comparable to primary BMDMs (Figures 1D–F). We next determined the role of TLRs, a PRR family that surveys for PAMPs in the extracellular and endosomal spaces1, in these bacteria-induced responses. To this end, we employed iBMDMs deficient in the proteins MyD88 and TRIF, which are defective for all TLR-dependent activities30, the specificity of which was confirmed using TLR and cytoplasmic PRR ligands (Figures S1E–F). We found that Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs were defective for TNFα secretion in response to all bacteria examined (Figure 1E), indicating that TLRs are the primary drivers of bacteria-induced TNFα production. In contrast, all bacteria examined induced IFN responses by 24 hours in Myd88−/−Trif−/− cells (Figures 1D–F). A multiplicity of infection (MOI) as low as 1 was sufficient for most bacteria to stimulate IFN responses, which were not associated with host cell death (Figures S1G–H). Diverse bacteria can therefore stimulate TLR-independent IFN responses.

### STING controls TLR-independent IFN responses to bacteria in macrophages.

We defined the genetic pathway important for TLR-independent IFN signaling using a refined group of bacteria and established positive roles for TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), IFN regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), and IFN-α/β receptor (IFNAR) (Figures S1I–P). To determine which PRR mediates bacteria-induced IFN responses, we first examined MAVS and RIP2, which regulate cytoplasmic RNA- and peptidoglycan-sensing, respectively2,31. These proteins were largely dispensable for IFN responses to bacteria (Figures S1Q–U).

We next examined a role for STING. STING drives IFN by detecting CDNs produced by bacteria or the CDN 2′3′-cGAMP (“2′3′-cGA”), which is synthesized by cGAS upon cGAS recognition of cytosolic DNA3,32. Bacterial exposure to Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs resulted in increased abundance of activated STING (STING S365 phosphorylation, “pSTING”) (Figure 2A). Exposure of cells to all bacteria in our panel revealed an ablation of IFNβ and IP-10 secretion in Myd88−/−Trif−/−Sting−/− iBMDMs, compared to Myd88−/−Trif−/− cells (Figures 2B–C and S2A).

To determine the interplay between STING and TLRs, we generated Sting-deficiency in WT iBMDM and human THP-1 macrophage backgrounds (Figure S2A). Human and mouse STING were required for IFNβ and/or IP-10 secretion in response to all examined gram-positive bacteria but were dispensable for IFN responses to gram-negative bacteria (Figures 2D–F). STING chemical inhibition in WT iBMDMs or primary BMDMs also resulted in reduced IFN responses to gram-positive, but not gram-negative, bacteria (Figures S2B–E). STING depletion or inhibition resulted in modest reductions in TNFα secretion (Figures S2F–H). Bacterial survival and association with cells in all genotypes was comparable (Figure S2I–J). In addition, intraperitoneal injection of Listeria innocua in Stinggt/gt mice, which produce a null Sting allele33, resulted in reduced peritoneal pSTAT1 and viperin abundance, compared with WT mice (Figure 2G). IFN responses during peritoneal injections of Staphylococcus epidermidis, Lactococcus lactis, and Lactobacillus plantarum relied on STING, albeit the range of STING dependence varied (Figure S2K). Neither bacterial survival nor IL-6 secretion were affected by Sting-deficiency in vivo (Figures S2L–M). STING is therefore the principal mediator of IFN responses to gram-positive bacteria, even under conditions where TLR signaling is possible.

STING can detect CDNs produced by bacteria or cGAS. Cgas deficiency in WT or Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs resulted in an expected loss in IFNβ and IP-10 secretion to cytosolic DNA but normal IFN responses to the direct STING agonist ADU-S100 (Figures 2H–K and S2N)34. Cgas−/− or Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/− iBMDMs were also defective for IFNβ and IP-10 secretion in response to several bacteria. However, cGAS was largely dispensable for IFN responses to Staphylococcus aureus, L. innocua, and L. lactis. We next studied a panel of 25 additional gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, which includes common human microbiota (Figure S2O). All bacteria stimulated IP-10 secretion in WT and Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs (Figure 2L and S2P). While Sting-deficiency in Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs resulted in loss of IP-10 secretion to all bacteria tested, cGAS contributed variably.

To broadly define the role of these PRRs, we performed kinetic RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) during bacterial infection of WT and Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs with Cgas- or Sting-deficiency. Each bacterium examined stimulated canonical inflammatory gene expression that dominated at 4 hours and was less robust in Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs (Figure 2M). In contrast, by 8 and 16 hours, when canonical inflammatory gene expression waned, expression of ISGs was pronounced. At peak ISG expression (8 hours), Sting-deficiency resulted in a global reduction in ISG expression upon any infection (Figures 2M–N). Cgas-deficiency resulted in a global reduction in ISG expression upon infection with S. epidermidis and to a lesser extent with S. aureus or L. innocua, which both stimulate STING directly (Figure 2N). TLR-independent, STING-dependent IFN responses are therefore a common feature of host-bacteria interactions.

To determine whether bacteria dually stimulate cGAS and STING, we utilized a STING allele containing an R231H mutation, which detects the cGAS-derived CDN, 2′3′-cGA, but not the bacterial CDNs c-di-AMP (“3′3′-cAA”) and c-di-GMP (“3′3′-cGG”)35. Myd88−/−Trif−/−Sting−/− iBMDMs expressing WT- or R231H-STING demonstrated that both genotypes of cells secreted IP-10 in response to S. aureus (Figures 2O and S2Q). In contrast, IP-10 secretion in response to L. innocua and L. lactis was defective in R231H-STING-expressing cells. Thus, while all bacteria examined in this assay stimulate STING directly, S. aureus also stimulates cGAS.

cGAS-independent STING stimulation suggests a bacterial CDN as the STING-stimulatory ligand. To test this, we examined a S. aureus mutant lacking the diadenylate cyclase DacA, which cannot synthesize 3′3′-cAA36,37. We also examined a phosphodiesterase gdpP mutant, which produces increased 3′3′-cAA36,37. 3′3′-cAA was undetectable in uninfected and ΔdacA-infected iBMDMs lysates (Figure 2P–Q). In contrast, 3′3′-cAA was detectable in macrophages infected with WT or, to an even greater extent, ΔgdpP S. aureus. We calculated 0.33 and 6.6 femtograms of 3′3′-cAA were inside each macrophage after exposure to WT and ΔgdpP S. aureus, respectively. The intracellular 3′3′-cAA levels with WT or ΔgdpP S. aureus infection was similar to intracellular 3′3′-cAA abundance after exogenous addition of pure 3′3′-cAA at a concentration of 10 μg/mL. In Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/− iBMDMs, ΔgdpP S. aureus also stimulated IP-10 secretion, compared to WT bacteria, while ΔdacA S. aureus failed to do so (Figure 2R). ΔdacA S. aureus stimulated IP-10 secretion from Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs, where cGAS is intact. These data suggest that bacteria-derived CDNs enable cGAS-independent STING activation.

While a single human STING allele (i.e., “WT” STING) is present in at least one copy in up to 90% of the population, several minor STING alleles exist with differential CDN-detecting abilities38–40. To test the CDN-detecting abilities of human STING alleles, we reconstituted Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/−Sting−/− iBMDMs with WT human STING or the R232H, R293Q, R71H_G230A (“HA”), or R71H_G230A_R293Q (“HAQ”) alleles (Figure S2R). S. aureus and L. lactis infection of iBMDMs expressing WT- or HAQ-STING, but not R232H- or R293Q-STING, induced IP-10 secretion, compared to Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/−Sting−/− parental iBMDMs (Figure 2S). Interestingly, bacterial stimulation of HA-STING-expressing iBMDMs induced nearly ten times more IP-10 secretion over WT-STING. These data indicate that human STING alleles can potentiate or dampen responses to CDN-producing bacteria.

### STING detection of CDN-producing bacteria occurs irrespective of virulence potential.

As the microbiota drives basal IFN in vivo41–47, we determined the link between STING and IFN activities in physiological settings. We examined IFN responses in colonic biopsies from healthy humans or inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients. Whereas pSTAT1 and viperin were detected in colonic biopsy lysates from healthy individuals, IBD lysates displayed an enhanced IFN response (Figure S3A). To assess the genetic requirement for STING on basal IFN activities, we examined splenic lysates from WT mice, which displayed evidence of basal viperin abundance that was diminished in lysates from Stinggt/gt mice (Figures S3B–C). Homogenates from the spleen, cecum, liver, and lung of WT mice were assessed for the presence of four bacterial-derived CDNs, 3′3′-cGAMP (“3′3′-cGA”), 3′2′-cGAMP (“3′2′-cGA”), 3′3′-cAA, and 3′3′-cGG, as well as the host-derived CDN, 2′3′-cGA, which can also be synthesized by bacteria48,49. In the mouse cecum, we observed a high abundance of CDNs dominated by 3′3′-cGG, followed by a lesser abundance of 3′3′-cAA and 3′3′-cGA and a minor representation by 3′2′-cGA and 2′3′-cGA (Figure 3A). We observed less CDN abundance in the spleen, liver, and lung, and 3′3′-cGA and 3′3′-cAA were the dominant detectable CDNs (Figures 3B–D). In the spleen, cGAS-derived 2′3′-cGA was not detectable, pointing to bacterial-derived CDNs as the relevant activators of basal STING activities in the spleen (Figures 3C and S3B–C). We observed a similar diverse spectrum of CDNs in healthy human feces with increased abundance in IBD patient feces (Figure 3E). These findings highlight the prolific nature of bacteria-derived CDNs in healthy and diseased tissues, which correlates with STING-driven IFN activities.

To determine if pathogenic bacteria can stimulate STING, even if rendered avirulent, we examined pathogens that have been genetically modified to remove their membranolytic activities. We first studied the pathogen Listeria monocytogenes. STING-dependent IFN to L. monocytogenes requires escape from phagosomes as mediated by the cytolysin, Listeriolysin O (LLO, encoded by the hly gene) and two phospholipases, PlcA and PlcB33,50–55. At 4 hours post-infection, only WT L. monocytogenes, but not the ΔhlyΔplcAΔplcB mutant or L. innocua which does not encode for hly or escape from phagosomes56, stimulated STAT1 activation and viperin production by iBMDMs (Figure 3F). Interestingly, by extending the infection to 24 hours, all Listeria strains induced cGAS-independent, STING-dependent IFN responses from Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs (Figures 3F–G).

We next examined the STING-stimulatory, pore-forming toxin producers Streptococcus pyogenes and S. aureus57–59. We found that a S. pyogenes mutant lacking its cytolysin streptolysin O (SLO), termed Δslo, stimulated TLR-independent, STING-dependent IP-10 secretion, albeit a higher MOI for Δslo was needed to yield equivalent IP-10 secretion to WT bacteria (Figure 3H). These data correspond with our findings using several commensal Streptococci, which do not encode slo, and yet stimulate STING (Figures 2L and S2P). Parental S. aureus and a strain lacking all major pore-forming toxins, termed Δtoxins60, also stimulated comparable cGAS-independent, STING-dependent IP-10 secretion (Figure 3I).

Finally, we performed studies with a strain of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis that encodes a membrane-damaging type 3 secretion system (T3SS) but lacks the effectors that modulate immune signaling61–63. We engineered this strain to produce S. aureus DacA to synthesize 3′3′-cAA (Figure S3D). The parental strain of Y. pseudotuberculosis stimulated IP-10 secretion from Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs, by a process that required the T3SS, bacterial viability, cGAS and STING (Figure 3J). In contrast, Y. pseudotuberculosis::dacA+ stimulated IP-10 secretion in a STING-dependent (but cGAS-independent) manner, regardless of T3SS expression or bacterial viability. These collective findings indicate that membrane-damaging proteins can potentiate, but are not strictly required for, STING activation.

As a complementary approach to the above use of mutant pathogens, we engineered a simple, non-pathogenic laboratory strain of Escherichia coli to produce S. aureus DacA (Figure S3E). Parental E. coli stimulated modest IP-10 secretion from Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs in a manner requiring cGAS and STING (Figure 3K). In contrast, E. coli::dacA+ stimulated cGAS-independent, STING-dependent IP-10 secretion in Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs. WT and Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs exposed to E. coli::dacA+ exhibited increased detection of pSTING, pSTAT1, and viperin, compared to uninfected cells (Figure 3L). DacA production in a strain of E. coli whose LPS stimulates TLR4 poorly64 also increased IP-10 secretion from WT and Cgas−/−, but not Sting−/−, iBMDMs (Figures 3M and S3F). Decreasing IPTG in E. coli::dacA+ resulted in a step-wise decrease in DacA abundance and IP-10 secretion from infected Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/− iBMDMs (Figure S3G–H). Similarly, decreased MOIs diminished the extent of IP-10 secretion from these cells (Figure S3I). However, an MOI as low as 0.1 still induced robust IP-10 production (~25 ng from ~106 cells). To confirm a role for DacA enzymatic activity, we generated E. coli expressing catalytically inactive dacA mutants65,66. 3′3′-cAA was only detected from lysed E. coli producing WT-DacA or lysed WT-DacA-infected macrophages (Figures 3N–P). Only WT-DacA-producing E. coli stimulated IP-10 secretion from Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/− iBMDMs (Figure 3Q). Similarly, only WT-DacA production in a strain of E. coli whose LPS cannot stimulate human TLR464 resulted in IP-10 secretion in WT or CGAS-deficient, but not STING1-deficient, human THP-1 macrophages (Figures 3R, S2A, and S3J). Thus, heterologous production of DacA is sufficient to elicit robust IFN responses and to convert non-pathogenic E. coli from a direct cGAS agonist to a direct STING agonist.

While S. aureus and E. coli::dacA+ bacterial infection stimulated IP-10 secretion from Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/− iBMDMs, conditioned culture supernatants from these bacteria failed to induce IP-10 secretion (Figure 3S). This finding suggests that intracellular bacteria are the source of CDNs that stimulate STING. Consistent with this idea, preventing phagocytosis of E. coli::dacA+ by cytochalasin D treatment inhibited IFN responses (Figures 3T–U). Cytochalasin D treatment failed to alter IFN responses to pure, exogenous CDNs or E. coli::dacA+ that was lysed prior to infection (Figure 3T, 3V). Cytochalasin D treatment also specifically prevented Ifnb1 expression by macrophages exposed to all examined bacteria that naturally stimulate cGAS and/or STING (Figure 3W). Thus, phagocytosis is required for STING activation in response to natural and bioengineered bacteria.

E. coli::dacA+ survived poorly within macrophages (Figure S3K), suggesting viability after phagocytosis is dispensable for STING activation. Indeed, live and dead E. coli::dacA+ stimulated comparable phagocytosis-dependent IFN responses from infected iBMDMs (Figure 3U and 3X). Using nine natural cGAS- and/or STING-stimulatory bacteria, we found that four species stimulated pSTAT1 and viperin abundance in Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs regardless of bacterial viability, whereas IFN responses to the others only partially required viability (Figure S3L). These findings suggest that active bacterial processes are often dispensable for STING detection.

We predicted bacterial CDNs are released after lysis in a mature phagolysosome. Treatment with ammonium chloride to neutralize acidification of the maturing phagolysosome failed to alter pSTAT1 and viperin abundance to DMXAA, a synthetic, membrane-permeant STING agonist (Figure 3Y). In contrast, ammonium chloride treatment reduced IFN responses to S. aureus or E. coli::dacA+. As a complementary approach, we examined a S. aureus autolysin mutant, Δatl, that has a reduced capacity to undergo lysis67. In Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs, Δatl S. aureus stimulated reduced pSTAT1 and viperin abundance, compared to WT S. aureus (Figure S3M). CDNs from intraphagosomal, lysed bacteria can therefore stimulate STING-dependent IFN responses.

### The CDN transporters SLC46A2 and LRRC8A mediate STING activation by bacteria.

Several membrane-spanning transport proteins can facilitate cytosolic entry of pure CDNs68. These include members of the solute carrier (SLC) transporter family and the volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) family13–17. All of these proteins are thought to function in CDN transport from the plasma membrane, yet their activities have only been documented using pure CDNs13–17. Curiously, the CDN transporters SLC46A1, SLC46A2, SLC46A3, and LRRC8A, as well as fluorescently-labelled CDNs, can all localize to the endosomal network11,69–72.

We first examined a role for SLCs 19A1, 46A1, 46A2, and 46A3, whose expression was detectable in WT and Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs, except for Slc46a2, as expected15 (Figure S4A). We generated SLC gene inactivation and overexpression lines in Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs and observed little effect of SLCs on IFN responses to bacteria (Figures S4B–I). An exception was with overexpression of Slc46a2, which increased IP-10, pSTING, and viperin abundance in response to pure 2′3′-cGA and the CDN-producing bacteria E. coli::dacA+, L. innocua, and L. lactis, but not to the membrane-permeant STING agonist DMXAA (Figures 4A–C). Thus, SLC46A2 is sufficient to mediate IFN responses to CDN-producing bacteria.

mRNA transcripts for all five leucine-rich repeat-containing protein 8 (LRRC8) VRAC components were detectable in WT and Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs (Figure S4A). As LRRC8A is an obligatory component of VRAC channels, we generated Myd88−/−Trif−/−Lrrc8a−/− iBMDMs (Figure S4J). As expected16,17, IP-10 secretion to 2′3′-cGA, but not DMXAA, was reduced in Myd88−/−Trif−/−Lrrc8a−/− iBMDMs, compared to Myd88−/−Trif−/− cells (Figure 4D). LRRC8A was also required for E. coli::dacA+ and the natural CDN-producing bacteria L. innocua and L. lactis to induce IP-10 secretion (Figures 4D–E). Kinetic RNA-seq analysis of Myd88−/−Trif−/− and Myd88−/−Trif−/−Lrrc8a−/− iBMDMs infected with L. innocua revealed a reliance on LRRC8A for ISG expression, which was most apparent at later time points (Figure 4F). LRRC8A was not required for IFN responses induced by S. aureus, which can stimulate cGAS or STING directly (Figure 4G–F). Thus, LRRC8A can mediate IFN responses to natural and bioengineered CDN-producing bacteria.

VRAC transport activities of 2′3′-cGA are enhanced under hypotonic conditions16,17. We therefore examined STING activation in iBMDMs cultured under physiologic and hypotonic, channel-gating conditions. Consistent with expectations16,17, hypotonic conditions enhanced the ability of exogenous 2′3′-cGA, but not DNA transfected into the cytosol, to activate STING and TBK1 (TBK1 S172 autophosphorylation, “pTBK1”), by a process that required LRRC8A (Figures S4K–L). We found that LRRC8A was similarly required for STING and TBK1 activation in response to E. coli::dacA+ under hypotonic conditions (Figures 4G–H and S4M–N). This finding was made with chemical inhibition of LRRC8A and Myd88−/−Trif−/−Lrrc8a−/− clones generated from two different CRISPR guides, as well as Lrrc8a-deficiency in Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/− iBMDM, WT iBMDM, and human THP-1 macrophage backgrounds (Figures 4G–H and S4M–O). Under hypotonic conditions, all iBMDM genotypes maintained ~90% viability, and LRRC8A did not impact the phagocytic capacity of cells (Figures S4P–R). As a complementary approach, we performed pulse-chase experiments where phagocytosis occurred in physiologic media, followed by culture in hypotonic media. In the extreme example of this pulse-chase regimen, a one-hour treatment with hypotonic media after three hours of host-bacteria interactions in physiological media was sufficient to reveal a requirement for LRRC8A for IFN responses to E. coli::dacA+ (Figure S4S). Similar findings were made with 2′3′-cGA, L. lactis, and ΔgdpP S. aureus (Figures 4I–J). Lrrc8a−/− iBMDMs reconstituted with Lrrc8a, but not empty vector, restored STING activation in response to E. coli::dacA+ under pulse-chase conditions (Figure 4K). We also found that genetic deficiency in Lrrc8a, but not other Lrrc8 genes, resulted in defective TBK1 activation in response to E. coli::dacA+ and 2′3′-cGA (Figure S4T).

As the above findings are consistent with the idea that LRRC8A mediates STING activation to bacteria downstream of phagocytosis, we manipulated phagosomes under hypotonic conditions. Treatment with cytochalasin D reduced TBK1 activation in response to E. coli::dacA+, but not 2′3′-cGA, in Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs under hypotonic conditions (Figure 4L). Furthermore, cells treated with bafilomycin A1, an inhibitor of phagosome acidification, prevented TBK1 activation in response to E. coli::dacA+, but not 2′3′-cGA, in Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs under hypotonic conditions (Figure 4M). These findings inform a model whereby CDN-producing bacteria are first internalized into bacteriolytic phagosomes, followed by STING activation mediated by the CDN transporters LRRC8A or SLC46A2. Notably, we found no evidence to suggest that LRRC8A, SLC46A2, or any other examined transporter are functionally redundant or operationally dependent on one another (Figures S4U–X). A context-dependent network of CDN transporters may therefore function to link phagosomal bacteriolysis to STING activation.

### Dead, CDN-laden bacteria as an engineering platform for cancer immunotherapy.

STING activity is positively correlated with anti-tumor immunity73. We reasoned that the use of dead non-pathogens should elicit STING-driven anti-tumor responses in vivo, without the risk of infection. To this end, we used a strain of E. coli (“ClearColi”), which poorly stimulates murine TLR4 to minimize LPS-TLR4 endotoxin activities64. We engineered ClearColi to produce WT or catalytically dead DacA as in Figure 3N–Q and anchored the antigen ovalbumin (OVA) into the outer membrane of ClearColi::dacA(WT)+ or ClearColi::dacA(RHR_AAA)+. Three hours after protein induction, bacteria were inactivated by PFA fixation (Figure S5A–B). These bacteria are referred to as “dacA(WT)” or “dacA(RHR_AAA)”.

We implanted B16-OVA melanoma tumors onto WT mice subcutaneously, and then treated palpable tumors with dacA(WT) or dacA(RHR_AAA) via three intratumoral (I.T.) injections (Figure 5A schematic). I.T. treatment with dacA(WT) significantly delayed and, in some mice, reversed B16-OVA tumor growth over time (Figure S5C). Correspondingly, I.T. treatment with dacA(WT) prolonged animal survival, compared to dacA(RHR_AAA) treatment (Figure 5A).

To determine if systemic treatments also offer protection, we treated mice with weekly retro-orbital (R.O.) injections starting six days after subcutaneous B16-OVA implantation (Figure 5B schematic). R.O. treatment with dacA(WT) delayed B16-OVA tumor size, compared to dacA(RHR_AAA) treatment (Figure S5D). In some mice treated with systemic dacA(WT), B16-OVA tumor growth was stalled until treatments were halted after 4 weeks (Figure S5D). This delayed growth of B16-OVA tumors upon systemic treatment with dacA(WT) corresponded to prolonged animal survival (Figure 5B).

Since dacA(WT) demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in an implantable tumor setting, we next tested systemic dacA(WT) treatment in a distinct genetically engineered mouse model of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) where tumor cells express OVA and luciferase, the latter serving as a bioluminescent readout of tumor burden74,75. Starting one day after tumor initiation, mice with equivalent baseline bioluminescent signal (Figure S5E) were treated bi-weekly with R.O. bacteria (Figure 5C schematic). Bioluminescent imaging of mice revealed decreased luciferase activity (reflective of tumor burden) with dacA(WT) treatment, compared to dacA(RHR_AAA) (Figure S5E). Mouse survival was also prolonged with dacA(WT)-treatment, compared to dacA(RHR_AAA) (Figure 5C). These results demonstrate that dead, CDN-laden bacteria can promote anti-tumor immunity with two different routes of injection and in two distinct tumor models.

Beyond treating established tumors, we tested whether these bacteria can elicit anti-tumor responses via a prophylactic vaccination approach. To this end, we treated WT mice with a single R.O. injection of dacA(WT), and five days later, we initiated HCC oncogenesis (Figure S5F schematic). While bioluminescent imaging of mice one day post-oncogenic initiation (i.e., six days post-dacA(WT) treatment) revealed similar luciferase activity between untreated and dacA(WT)-treated mice, we observed decreased luciferase activity as early as day eight in mice prophylactically treated with dacA(WT), compared to untreated mice (Figure S5G). Notably, 78% of untreated mice succumbed to tumor burden, while all dacA(WT)-treated mice survived for over 210 days (Figure S5F). Thus, a single prophylactic treatment with dead, CDN-laden bacteria is capable of driving anti-tumor immunity.

### Diverse CDN structures delivered by bacteria activate STING via SLC46A2 and LRRC8A.

Bacteria synthesize diverse CDNs in nature76,77. To examine bacterial delivery of other CDNs to STING, we generated a panel of E. coli engineered to produce 17 distinct CDN synthases with validated or predicted chemical structures (Table S2 and Figure S5H)3,49,78–88. Bacteria producing numerous CDNs stimulated STING-dependent IP-10 secretion, independent of cGAS (Figure 5D). Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis of bacterial lysates confirmed STING-stimulatory bacteria produced their predicted CDN and failure for engineered bacteria to stimulate STING was due to a failure in CDN production (Figure S5I and Table S2).

We selected bacteria producing S. aureus DacA (3′3′-cAA) or Crassostrea virginica cGLR1 (2′3′-cUMP-AMP, “2′3′-cUA”) for further analysis by RNA-seq. Bacteria producing 3′3′-cAA or 2′3′-cUA stimulated stronger ISG expression in WT or Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs, compared with parental bacteria, which occurred independently of cGAS but relied on STING (Figure 5E). Interestingly, CDN-producing bacteria suppressed the expression of a subset of canonical inflammatory genes in WT or Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs, as compared to parental bacteria. This suppression of inflammatory gene expression was also STING-dependent.

In contrast to bacteria producing WT enzymes, bacteria producing catalytic dead CDN synthases failed to stimulate IP-10 secretion in Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/− iBMDMs (Figures S5J–K). Phagocytosis, SLC46A2, and LRRC8A were important for mediating IFN responses to all examined engineered E. coli (Figures 5F–I and S5L). Structurally diverse CDNs can therefore be sourced from phagocytosed bacteria to activate STING in a manner supported by CDN transporters.

### Detection of diverse CDN structures, including pyrimidine-containing CDNs, is a primordial feature of animal STING.

Our analysis revealed stimulation of murine STING by bacteria producing the pyrimidine-containing CDN 2′3′-cUA (i.e., E. coli::CV-Cglr1+ and E. coli::CG-Cglr1+) (Figure 5). This finding was notable as pyrimidine-based CDNs are not considered mammalian STING agonists given their smaller size, compared to purines, that could limit adequate contact within the STING ligand binding pocket89,90. Questions also remain with regard to diverse CDN detection as a general feature of animal STINGs. We therefore defined the stimulatory capacity of diverse CDNs on diverse animal STING proteins.

We first reconstituted Sting-deficient iBMDMs with eight animal STINGs (Figure 6A). Macrophages producing STING from each species secreted increased IP-10 in response to 2′3′-cGA, compared to untreated cells (Figure 6B). Using seven additional CDNs from nature, we found that each species’ STING protein drove IP-10 secretion in macrophages exposed to diverse CDNs, including 2′3′-cUA (Figure 6B). While 2′3′-cGA and 3′3′-cGG were generally the most and least potent animal STING ligand, respectively, several animal STINGs responded to multiple CDNs in a manner comparable to 2′3′-cGA. These findings suggest that diverse CDN detection is conserved for animal STING.

Using THP-1 macrophages, we found that pure 2′3′-cUA and 2′3′-cUA-producing E. coli::CV-Cglr1+ stimulated STING and IFN responses (Figure S6A). At concentrations that we found corresponded to intracellular CDN levels present during bacterial infections (Figures 2P–Q), primary human monocyte treatment with pure 2′3′-cUA, 2′3′-cGA, and 3′3′-cAA, but not with 3′3′-cGG, increased IFN responses (Figures 6C, D). We were struck by the similar IFN response magnitude between cGAS-derived 2′3′-cGA compared to bacterial-derived 3′3′-cAA as the affinity of human STING for 2′3′-cGA (~3.79nM) is nearly 1,000-fold greater than its affinity for 3′3′-linked, bacterial-derived CDNs (>1μM)91. We performed a dose-titration experiment in primary human monocytes and found that, as expected, lower concentrations of 2′3′-cGA stimulated IFN responses, compared to 3′3′-cAA (Figures 6E and S6B). However, in contrast to their biochemical affinities91, the calculated EC50 of 2′3′-cGA-induced IP-10 secretion revealed that 2′3′-cGA was only ~4 times more potent than 3′3′-cAA (Figure 6E). We therefore conclude that STING from human cells strongly detects diverse CDNs, including 2′3′-cUA and select 3′3′-linked bacterial-derived CDNs.

Using Myd88−/−Trif−/−Cgas−/−Sting−/− iBMDMs reconstituted with WT, R232H, R293Q, HA, or HAQ human STING alleles (Figures 2S and S2R), we found that WT- and HAQ-STING mediated similar amounts of IP-10 secretion in response to various pure- or engineered bacteria-derived CDNs (Figures 6F–G). iBMDMs expressing R232H- and R293Q-STING secreted IP-10 largely in response to pure or bacteria-derived 2′3′-cGA, although a few other CDNs were detectable by R293Q-STING. HA-STING also drove increased IP-10 secretion to almost all CDNs examined, compared with WT-STING, including a notable sensitivity to 3′3′-cGG that was not observed for other STING alleles.

For symmetry with our human STING analyses, we examined the behavior of primary bovine peripheral blood mononuclear cells exposed to diverse CDNs. We observed ~100-fold increases in bovine Rsad2 to diverse CDNs, including 2′3′-cUA, with poor responses observed for 3′3′-cGG (Figure 6H). Similar to human and bovine STING, murine STING from Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs drove IP-10 secretion to diverse CDNs, including 2′3′-cUA, with dose-titration experiments revealing 2′3′-cGA and 3′3′-cGA as the most potent CDNs (Figures S6C, D).

While diverse CDNs were detectable by animal STINGs, not all cyclic nucleotides were STING-stimulating entities, for example the purine-based cyclic trinucleotide 3′3′3′-cAAG as reported (Figures 6H and S6C–D)80. Moreover, compared to 2′3′-cUA, at equivalent concentrations, 3′3′-cUA failed to stimulate animal STINGs (Figures 6F, 6H, and S6C–D). However, extension of 3′3′-cUA, but not 3′3′-cUU, exposure time in iBMDMs or transfection of iBMDMs with 3′3′-cUA revealed STING-dependent IFN activities (Figure 6I and S6E). Thus, in the context of pyrimidine-containing CDNs, STING sensing requires a mixture of purines and pyrimidines, and the single change from a 2′–5′-phosphodiester linkage to a 3′–5′-phosphodiester linkage dictates different STING signaling strengths. We used electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) analysis and found a dissociation constant of murine STING for 2′3′-cUA measured at 690 nM, which was more than 10 times stronger than the measured affinity for 3′3′-cUA, confirming signaling strength differences is related to STING-CDN binding (Figure 6J and S6F).

Intraperitoneal injection of 2′3′-cGA and 2′3′-cUA induced similarly increased STING-dependent peritoneal IFN responses, compared to PBS-treated mice (Figures 6K–M). Despite weak activities in vitro, 3′3′-cUA stimulated STING-dependent IFN activities in all mice, compared to PBS-treated mice, and in 5 of 8 of mice, IFN responses to 3′3′-cUA were comparable to those induced by 2′3′-cGA stimulation (Figure 6N). cUA molecules are therefore STING agonists in vivo.

### Differential interactions between STING and pyrimidine- and purine-based CDNs.

We determined a crystal structure of murine STING (mSTING) in complex with 2′3′-cUA (1.98 Å). For comparison, we determined a crystal structure of mSTING bound to 3′3′-cAA (1.22 Å) and analyzed the previously determined 1.77 Å mSTING–2′3′-cGA crystal structure92. All CDNs similarly bound STING in the “closed” conformation, characterized by a four-stranded antiparallel β sheet lid covering the CDN and a compact configuration between the two protomer wings that we measured at ~32–33 Å for each CDN (Figure 7A–B). We observed that several key contacts with STING were maintained across all CDNs, including Y166, R237, and V238 (Figure 7C–D).

In contrast to these commonalities, different contacts between mSTING and 2′3′-cUA were observed in comparison with 2′3′-cGA and 3′3′-cAA. One difference lies in the lack of contacts between S161 and 2′3′-cUA, which are present in the mSTING–2′3′-cGA and mSTING–3′3′-cAA structures (Figure 7D). While the 2′3′-cUA uracil directly contacts T262, this T262 contact is water-mediated in the mSTING–3′3′-cAA structure and absent in the mSTING–2′3′-cGA structure. We also observed a difference in the symmetry of protomer contacts between CDNs. Whereas T266, Y239, S240, and R231 from each protomer forms contacts with 2′3′-cGA and 3′3′-cAA, only a single protomer contributes the analogous contact with 2′3′-cUA. We also determined the crystal structure of mSTING bound to 3′3′-cUA (1.83 Å), which reproduced most of the mSTING–2′3′-cUA structural features (Figure S7A–C). These observations demonstrate that STING recognition of CDNs can withstand extensive asymmetry in protomer contacts.

To test the importance of STING-CDN interactions, we reconstituted Myd88−/−Trif−/−Sting−/− iBMDMs with WT STING and 11 different STING variants mutated for single amino acid residues (Figure S7D). We targeted residues that exhibited direct or water-mediated contacts with CDNs92–94. We confirmed the critical roles of Y162, Y166, R237, Y239, and E259 in mediating STING detection of any CDN (Figure 7E). In contrast, cells reconstituted with R231H-STING or N241A-STING detected 2′3′-cGA but were largely unable to detect any other CDN, including the linkage isomer 3′2′-cGA. Alanine substitution of I229, V238, S240, or T262 STING residues yielded reductions in IP-10 secretion only to select CDNs, including 2′3′-cUA, 3′3′-cAA, and 3′3′-cGG. These collective results demonstrate the mechanisms underlying detection of diverse CDNs.

## Discussion

Based on the data presented herein, we propose that the versatility of STING as a generic sensor of bacteria is enabled by its ability to detect CDNs beyond 2′3′-cGA synthesized by cGAS. As we found that diverse animal STINGs detect diverse CDNs, including pyrimidine-containing CDNs, we propose that the ability of animal STING to detect diverse CDNs could be an evolutionarily-driven adaptation. In contrast to the flexible nature of animal STING for its CDN ligands, bacterial STING proteins detect a single CDN structure88. Nevertheless, the existence of STING in bacteria as a phage defense element is one of many examples of the ancient origins of innate immunity. It is notable to consider that STING was first discovered in eukaryotes, prior to its prokaryotic origins being identified. Similar statements apply to the phage defense activities of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor/resistance domain-based proteins, viperins, NOD-related proteins, and gasdermins95,96, all of which were first defined in eukaryotes. However, our finding of a stimulatory activity for cUA inverts this eukaryote→prokaryote discovery pipeline, as cUA was first defined as a component of innate immunity in bacteria80,81. cUA therefore represents an interesting example of how the study of phage defense has informed our understanding of mammalian innate immunity, rather than vice versa.

A notable aspect of our study is the finding that pyrimidine-containing CDNs bind STING in a unique manner that results in STING activation. Our structural analyses revealed several asymmetric protomer contacts in mSTING–2′3′-cUA and mSTING–3′3′-cUA that were symmetrical for purine-based CDNs. The reduced size of the uracil pyrimidine, compared to purines, may account for this impaired symmetrical interaction within the binding pocket. In spite of this asymmetry, 2′3′-cUA, and to a lesser extent the isomer 3′3′-cUA, stimulated STING signaling comparable to purine-based CDNs. Indeed, in humans, 2′3′-cUA was a more potent STING agonist than the di-purine 3′3′-cGG, and in mice, 2’3’-cUA had the highest affinity for STING than any CDN examined other than cGA linkage isomers. Other linkage isomers differ in STING stimulatory activities, as is the case for 2′3′-cGA that has stronger affinity for STING than 3′3′-cGA91. This observation may be explained by the increased flexibility of a 3′3′-macrocyclic phosphodiester ring, compared to a 2′3′-macrocyclic phosphodiester ring97. As a consequence of its structural rigidity, 2′3′-cGA has a higher likelihood of existing in an energetically favorable “U-shape”, which is found for all STING-bound CDNs98. Nevertheless, all purine-based linkage isomers stimulate STING signaling. We therefore propose a revised model for constraints on CDN-mediated STING signaling, whereby STING detection of CDNs can withstand the presence of a flexible 3′3′-macrocyclic phosphodiester ring or a reduced CDN size, but both of these features at once reduce STING-CDN detection. These studies expand our understanding of how the versatile PRR STING can detect its CDN PAMP ligand, and provide a mandate to expand the contexts in which STING may contribute to host-bacteria encounters.

### Limitation of the Study

This study demonstrates the versatility of STING as a common sensor of diverse bacteria by defining a phagosomal CDN-transporter-STING axis and broadening the spectrum of CDN species detectable by animal STING proteins. However, several limitations of this study should be noted. For example, these studies largely employ the use of in vitro macrophage infections. Thus, while STING detection of diverse bacteria and CDNs, such as cUA molecules, is possible as demonstrated by our in vivo studies, it remains unclear when and how bacterial CDNs are delivered to STING in an animal during commonplace interactions with bacteria (i.e., those interactions with commensal non-pathogens). Moreover, while we detected several diverse CDNs in mice, as well as in healthy and diseased humans, it remains unclear when many of the examined CDNs of this study, including pyrimidine-based CDNs, are naturally produced by bacteria and how much these CDNs impact STING activities in animals. Further studies examining bacterial CDN production and STING activities in vivo are needed to address these limitations.

For primary bone marrow-derived macrophages, L929 cells were grown to confluency, incubated for 48 hrs, and M-CSF-containing supernatants were then collected and passaged through a 0.22 μm filter. At day 3, 5 mL of differentiation medium was added. At day 6, cells were lifted with 1xPBS supplemented with 2.5 mM EDTA, centrifuged at 400xg 5 min, and the pellet resuspended in differentiation medium with reduced L929 supernatant (i.e., DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1x antibiotic/antimycotic, and 5% L929 supernatant) at a concentration of 0.5×106 cells/mL. 1 mL BMDMs were plated in each well of a 24-well TC-treated plate and allowed to adhere overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. Prior to infection, BMDM supernatants were aspirated from each well and 1 mL DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 5% L929 supernatant was added to each well and remained present throughout the experiment.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### CRISPR-mediated gene inactivation

To inactivate genes in WT and Myd88−/−Trif−/− iBMDMs or WT human THP-1 cells via CRISPR-Cas9, guide oligos targeting genes of interest were designed with CRISPick (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public) and are listed in Table S3. One guide targeting murine Sting1 was previously published108. Guide sequences were incorporated into sense and antisense oligos with the appropriate Esp3I overhangs on the 5′ end (e.g., sense oligo: 5′ CACCGNx20 3′, where CACC corresponds to the 5’ Esp3I overhang, G helps with guide transcription, and Nx20 is the 20 nucleotide guide sequence) and 3′ end (e.g., antisense oligo: 5′ AAACNx20C 3′, where AAAC is the 3’ Esp3I overhang, Nx20 is the reverse complement of the 20 nucleotide guide sequence, and C base pairs with G in the sense oligo). To phosphorylate and anneal guide oligos, 2μL each of 50 μM sense and 50 μM antisense oligos were mixed with 1X T4 ligase buffer (NEB #B0202S) and 0.5μL T4 polynucleotide kinase (NEB #M0201S) for a total 10 μL reaction. The reaction mixture was incubated in a thermal cycler with the following steps: 1) 37°C for 30 min, 2) 95°C for 5 min, 3) 2°C/sec decrease to 85°C, 4) 85°C for 1 min, and 5) 0.1°C/sec decrease to 25°C. Phosphorylated, annealed oligos were diluted 1:20 in molecular grade H2O and then ligated into Esp3I-digested pLentiCRISPR V2.0 (Addgene #52961). Ligation reactions were then transformed into Top10 competent E. coli (Thermo Fisher Scientific #C404010) and selected with 100 μg/mL ampicillin.

To transduce iBMDMs or THP-1s with lentivirus, 2.5×106 HEK293T cells were seeded into a 10 cm TC-treated dish and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. HEK293T cells were then transfected with a mixture of 10 μg of pLentiCRISPR containing the CRISPR guide of interest, 10 μg of psPAX2 lentiviral packing plasmid, and 2.5 μg pCMV-VSV-G with Opti-MEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific # 31985062) and Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific #11668019) according to manufacturer’s instructions. After an overnight incubation of the transfection at 37°C with 5% CO2, supernatants were aspirated from transfected cells, 6 mL cDMEM added for iBMDMs transfections or 6 mL cRPMI added for THP-1 transfections, and cells incubated for 24 hrs at 37°C with 5% CO2. 0.5×106 iBMDMs were plated per well of a 6-well TC plate and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. 0.5×106 THP-1 cells were plated per well of a 12-well TC plate. 24 hr viral particle-laden supernatants were harvested, centrifuged at 400xg 5 min, passaged through a 0.45 μm filter, and mixed with 0.05% v/v Polybrene (Millipore TR-1003-G). iBMDM supernatants were aspirated and cells exposed to the prepared virus mixture and centrifuged at 1250xg 1 hr at 30°C. Transduced cells were allowed to rest with added cDMEM or cRPMI for 24 hrs, and then cells were subjected to one more round of viral transduction. After 24 hrs rest, cells were exposed to cDMEM supplemented with 4–10 μg/mL puromycin for iBMDMs or cRPMI supplemented with 1 μg/mL puromycin for THP-1s for one week to select for transduced cells. To harvest single CRISPR gene inactivation clonal iBMDMs, puromycin-selected cells were diluted to 1 cell per well in a 96-well TC-treated plate and allowed to propagate. Where possible, clones were confirmed as having gene inactivation via loss of protein expression by immunoblot. In the case of IFNAR1 gene inactivation, clones were screened by the absence of IP-10 secretion in response to recombinant IFNβ. In contexts where antibodies do not exist, clones were confirmed by genomic DNA sequencing and analyzed for gene inactivation status by ICE (https://ice.synthego.com/).

#### Cloning into overexpression vectors

To create engineered E. coli, gBlocks of CDN synthases were designed with a 5′ BamHI site, a C-terminal 3x-FLAG tag, and a 3′ EcoRI site, and were codon optimized for expression in E. coli (see Table S2 for the accession number for each protein sequence)109. gBlocks were digested with BamHI and EcoRI and ligated into pET28a(+) vector lacking a His-Tag110, which contains an IPTG-inducible lac promoter. Rosetta(DE3)pLysS E. coli or ClearColi were transformed with a modified and transformants selected with 50 μg/mL kanamycin and 25 μg/mL chloramphenicol. ClearColi were transformed with pET28a(+) constructs according to manufacturer’s instructions and selected with 50 μg/mL kanamycin. To create YP::dacA+, dacA-1xFLAG was PCR amplified from pET28a(+)-dacA-3xFLAG with the forward primer 5′ ACCGCCATATGGATTTCTCTAACTTCTTCC 3′ (NdeI site is underlined) and the reverse primer 5′ CAGCCGGATCCCTACTTATCGTCGTCATC 3′ (BamHI site is underlined) and subcloned into the pET16b with NdeI and BamHI restriction sites. Y. pseudotuberculosis was electroporated with the resulting pET16b-dacA-1xFLAG as described in111 and clones selected for with 100 μg/mL ampicillin. For cloning into pET16b as above, the construct has a 5′ NdeI site followed by the Sec signal sequence (for entry into the periplasm), then a myc tag sequence, a short random linker sequence, the natural OVA sequence truncated to only contain MHC peptides I and II, the AIDA-I sequence, and a 3′ BamHI site. To generate ClearColi producing DacA-3XFLAG (WT or RHR_AAA variants in pET28a(+) vectors) and myc-OVA-AIDA-I (pET16b), transformants were selected using 100 μg/mL ampicillin and 50 μg/mL kanamycin.

For macrophage gene reconstitution experiments, gBlocks were designed with a 5′ XhoI site, a C-terminal 3x-FLAG tag or left untagged as in the case for mouse Sting constructs, and a 3′ NotI site, and gBlocks were codon optimized for expression in M. musculus. #### Bacterial infections and treatments of macrophages

To culture bacteria for infections, S. aureus (SA113), S. capitis, S. caprae, S. epidermidis, and E. coli (K12, ClearColi, Rosetta, and Nissle) single colonies were inoculated into liquid LB (Miller LB for ClearColi) and grown overnight aerobically at 37°C. USA300 strains of S. aureus, S. carnosus, S. lugdunensis, and S. saprophyticus single colonies were inoculated into liquid TSB and grown overnight aerobically at 37°C with the exception that ΔdacA was grown in liquid TSB with a total of 0.8M NaCl. For Rosetta E. coli, 25 μg/mL chloramphenicol (to select for pLysS) and/or 50 μg/mL kanamycin (to select for pET28a(+) constructs) were used throughout growth. For ClearColi, 50 μg/mL kanamycin (to select for pET28a(+) constructs) or 50 μg/mL kanamycin and 100 μg/mL ampicillin (to select for pET28a(+) and pET16b double producing bacteria) were used throughout growth. To induce protein expression, E. coli and ClearColi were treated with isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG, Thermo Fisher Scientific # 15529019) at indicated concentrations (.01–1 mM) for 3 hrs just prior to infection. L. innocua, L. monocytogenes, C. pseudodiphtheriticum, C. xerosis, S. salivarius, S. mutans, S. gallolyticus, E. casseliflavus, E. saccharolyticus, and E. faecalis single colonies were inoculated into liquid BHI and grown overnight aerobically at 37°C. L. lactis colonies were inoculated into liquid BHI supplemented with 0.042% w/v NaHCO3, and grown overnight aerobically at 37°C. L. plantarum, L. rhamnosus, L. reuteri, L. gasseri, L. murinus, L. johnsonii, L. acidophilus, and L. delbrueckii single colonies were inoculated into liquid MRS supplemented with 0.042% w/v NaHCO3, and grown overnight aerobically at 37°C. B. subtilis and M. luteus single colonies were inoculated into liquid BHI and TSB, respectively, and grown overnight aerobically at 30°C. Approximately 15 N. perflava colonies were inoculated onto GCB agar, grown overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2, and stationary phase bacteria swabbed into liquid gonococcal media (1.5% w/v proteose peptone #3, 0.4% w/v K2HPO4, 0.1% w/v KH2PO4, and 0.1% w/v NaCl, pH 7.2) modified with Kellogg’s supplements and 0.042% w/v NaHCO3. Y. pseudotuberculosis single colonies were inoculated into liquid 2xYT and grown overnight aerobically at 26°C. YP::dacA+ bacteria were treated with 100 μg/mL ampicillin throughout growth. S. maltophila, K. aerogenes, and P. putida single colonies were inoculated into liquid Nutrient Broth and grown overnight aerobically at 37°C, 30°C, or 26°C, respectively. V. natriegens colonies were inoculated into liquid Nutrient Broth (1.5% NaCl supplement) and grown overnight aerobically at 26°C. P. damnosus single colonies were inoculated into liquid MRS and grown overnight aerobically at 26°C. S. pyogenes single colonies were inoculated into liquid THB supplemented with 0.2% yeast extract and 0.042% w/v NaHCO3 and statically grown overnight at 37°C.

To enrich for highly viable, logarithmic phase cultures that were used for infections, stationary phase bacteria in liquid cultures (i.e., overnight liquid cultures from above) were then subjected to two back dilutions and aerobic growth cycles under the above conditions (for M. luteus and P. damnosus, one back dilution). For S. pyogenes, overnight cultures were back-diluted 1:20 in THB supplemented with 0.2% yeast extract and 0.042% w/v NaHCO3 and statically grown at 37°C for 4 hours. For Y. pseudotuberculosis, overnight cultures were subsequently back diluted and induced for expression of the type 3 secretion system as previously described114. For YP::dacA+ experiments, parent and YP::dacA+ were grown as before except in LB. For non-inducing type 3 secretion system conditions, parent and YP::dacA+ overnight cultures were back diluted into LB and grown for 3 hrs aerobically at 37°C; all conditions received 1 mM IPTG during this 3 hr period. Approximately 15 B. fragilis and B. thetaiotaomicron colonies were inoculated onto agar as described above for 48 hrs anaerobically prior to being swabbed into BHI liquid media for its immediate use in infections.

At the time of infection, bacteria were centrifuged at 10,000xg 3 min, supernatant discarded, and pellets suspended in DMEM supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated FBS, 1x L-glutamine (#25030–081), 1x sodium pyruvate (#11360–070), herein referred to as “infection DMEM” (iDMEM). Bacteria suspended in iDMEM were plated to confirm multiplicity of infection (MOI). To prepare iBMDMs for infections, cultured iBMDMs were centrifuged at 400xg 5 min, the pellet resuspended to a concentration of 0.5×106 cells/mL in iDMEM, and 1 mL or 0.2 mL cells was seeded into each well of a 24-well or 96-well TC-treated plate, respectively. Seeded iBMDMs were allowed to adhere for at least 4 hrs at 37°C with 5% CO2. To initiate a synchronous infection, adherent iBMDMs were placed on ice for 5 min, supernatants aspirated, and then cells in the 24-well plate setup were exposed to 1 mL bacteria at the indicated MOI or 1 mL PAMPs at the indicated concentration. Cells were centrifuged at 400xg 5 min 4°C to initiate bacterial contact with iBMDMs. The infection was incubated for 1 hr at 37°C with 5% CO2 to allow for phagocytosis, after which infected supernatants were aspirated to remove non-adherent, extracellular bacteria. cDMEM containing 1x pen/strep was then added to eliminate remaining extracellular bacteria, and the infection was allowed to proceed at 37°C with 5% CO2 for the total indicated time. For experiments with inhibitors or BMDMs, pen/strep at a final concentration of 1x was spiked into cells to inactivated extracellular bacteria.

In cases where bacteria were inactivated prior to infection, including in vivo cancer treatments, pellets containing 1×108 colony forming unit (CFU) (as grown above) were resuspended in 1 mL 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in 1x PBS and incubated for 15 min at room temperature. PFA-inactivated bacteria were then centrifuged at 10,000xg 3 min, PFA supernatants removed, and pellets washed with 1 mL 1xPBS. After one more centrifugation step, the pellet of PFA-inactivated bacteria was resuspended in iDMEM (or 1xPBS for in vivo experiments) and plated to confirm bacterial inactivation.

To determine recoverable CFU during infection, iBMDMs were infected with an MOI of 50 as above. The inoculum was serially diluted and plated for viable CFU to determine starting CFU/mL. After 1 h infection, infection supernatants were removed and replaced with cDMEM and pen/strep. After 4 hrs or 24 hrs, supernatants were removed from infected iBMDMs, and cells were lysed with 200 μL 1% saponin (Sigma #47036) per well of a 24-well plate for 10 min at 37°C. 800 μL LB were then added to each well and mixed vigorously. Lysates were serially diluted and plated for viable CFU.

For cell association experiments by flow cytometry, bacteria were labelled with 5-(and-6)-carboxyfluorescein diacetate, succinimidyl ester (CFSE) as in115 and exposed to macrophages as above. After 2 hrs total incubation, macrophage supernatants were aspirated, cells washed once with 1 mL 1xPBS, and then cells lifted with 1xPBS with 2.5 mM EDTA. Cells were then centrifuged at 400xg 5 min, supernatants aspirated, and cells fixed with 1% PFA in 1xPBS. Data were acquired on a LSRFortessa™ cell analyzer (BD) and analyzed using FlowJo.

For experiments using bacterial conditioned supernatants, S. aureus and E. coli::dacA+ were grown as above, except with the following modification at the final back dilution step: 2 mL mid-log phase culture was centrifuged at 10,000xg 3 min, the pellet resuspended in 16 mL iDMEM (without phenol red) with 0.01 mM IPTG, and cultured aerobically for 3 hrs 37°C. Live bacteria were prepared as normally done above from these cultures. The remaining cultures were then equilibrated to an equivalent OD600 with iDMEM, centrifuged at 4,122xg 5 min, the supernatants passaged through a 0.22 μm filter, and 1 mL supernatants were applied to 0.5×106 macrophages per well. For experiments using bacterial lysates, ClearColii::dacA+ were grown as above, and a pellet of 8×108 CFU was resuspended with 40 μL bacterial protein extraction reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific #78243) and incubated 1 hr at room temperature with intermittent vortexing. 10 μL of this lysate was used to spike into 1 mL of adherent cells.

For SeV infection, SeV was diluted in DMEM supplemented with 1% FBS in a total volume of 100 μL per well (24-well plate format) for an MOI of 0.00001. iBMDMs were exposed to SeV for 1 hr at 37°C with 5% CO2 during which plates were gently rocked every 10 min. After 1 hr, supernatants were removed, replaced with 1 mL cDMEM, and infection incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2 for total indicated time.

All PAMPs were diluted in iDMEM to the indicated concentration before exposure to macrophages. For cytosolic transfections of PAMPs, 1 μg CT DNA, 100 μg CDNs (where indicated), or 0.5 μg 5′ppp-dsRNA was incubated with Opti-MEM and 3 μL Lipofectamine-2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific #11668019) for a total of 100 μL for at least 20 min prior to infection. Supernatants from macrophages were aspirated and 900 μL iDMEM added to each well, followed by 100 μL drop-wise addition of PAMPs for a final concentration of 1 μg/mL CT DNA, 100 μg/mL CDNs, or 0.5 μg/mL 5′ppp-dsRNA per well.

For cytochalasin D treatment, iBMDMs were treated with vehicle (DMSO) or 10 μg/mL cytoD for 10 min prior to and throughout infection. For the H-151 STING inhibitor, macrophages were treated with vehicle (DMSO) or 0.5 μg/mL (iBMDMs) or 1 μg/mL (BMDMs) H-151 for 1 hr prior to and throughout infection. For LRRC8A inhibition via DCPIB, iBMDMs were treated with vehicle (DMSO) or 20 μM DCPIB for 30 min prior to and throughout infection. For phagosome acidification inhibition, iBMDMs were treated with vehicle (DMSO) or 100 μM Bafilomycin A1 for 30 min prior to and throughout infection, or treated with LAL water (Invivogen) or 20 mM ammonium chloride for 30 min prior to and throughout infection.

For assessment of phagocytosis by immunofluorescence, E. coli-infected cells (MOI of 10) were stained as in116. Briefly, 10 min synchronously infected cells were fixed with 4% PFA for 15 min, washed 3 times with 1xPBS for 5 min each, blocked with 2% normal goat serum-1xPBS Jackson Laboratory (#005–000-121) for 1 hr, stained with anti-E. coli antibody (1:50 dilution) in 2% normal goat serum-1xPBS overnight at 4°C to label extracellular bacteria, washed as before, stained with goat anti-rabbit Alexa Flour 568 (Thermo Fisher Scientific #A11011) for 1 hr, and washed as before. Cells were then fixed again, washed, and permeabilized with 2% normal goat serum-1xPBS with 0.2% saponin for 1 hr. Cells were then stained with anti-E. coli antibody (1:50 dilution) in 2% normal goat serum-1xPBS with 0.2% saponin overnight at 4°C to label total bacteria, washed as before, stained with goat anti-rabbit Alexa Flour 488 (Thermo Fisher Scientific #A11008) and Alexa Flour phalloidin-647 (Thermo Fisher Scientific #A22287) for 1 hr, washed as before, exposed to DAPI (Biotium #40043) for 5 min, rinsed with water, and mounted with prolong antifade (Thermo Fisher Scientific #P36980). Images were acquired using a Zeiss 880 laser scanning confocal microscope.

For experiments using defined hypotonic medium (i.e., Figure S4K only), the hypotonic solution was made with endotoxin-free molecular grade water (Thermo Fisher Scientific #10–977-023) and the following defined solutes: 16.17 mM NaCl (Sigma #S8776), 6 mM KCl (Sigma #P9327–100ML), 1 mM MgCl2 (Thermo Fisher Scientific #AM9530G), 1.5 mM CaCl2 (Sigma, #C-34006), 10 mM glucose (Thermo Fisher Scientific #A2494001), 10 mM Hepes pH7.4 (Thermo Scientific Fisher #J16924.AP). For all other experiments, hypotonic conditions were created by diluting DMEM 1:4 with endotoxin-free molecular grade water (Thermo Fisher Scientific #10–977-023). For THP-1 macrophages, hypotonic conditions were created by diluting RPMI diluted with water as above.

The bacterial pellets were lysed with 200 μL bacterial protein extraction reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific #78243), and lysates were passaged through a 22g needle four times to reduce viscosity. #### Bulk RNA sequencing

Macrophages (untreated or infected as above) were lysed and RNA prepared as above, except that RNA was treated using Turbo DNase (Thermo Fisher Scientific #AM1907) according to manufacturer’s instructions for routine DNase treatment. Data from Illumina RNA sequencing (Azenta Life Sciences) was analyzed using the Galaxy Server118. Briefly, reads were cut and trimmed using fastp (quality phred set to 20, trim with the Illumina adaptors (R1: AGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAACTCCAGTCA and R2: AGATCGGAAGAGCGTCGTGTAGGGAAAGAGTGT), enabled UMI processing of Index1). Trimmed reads were aligned to the mm10 genome using RNA STAR. BAM files were used in featureCounts to generate count files, which were then placed into DeSeq2 to generate differentially expressed gene lists and normalized count files. Genes of interest were refined based on the DEG lists for all comparisons and those genes with an adjusted p-value < 0.01 and a log2 absolute value > 1. For display as heatmaps, the RNA-seq data was mapped against a published group of canonical inflammatory genes (344 total)119–122, as well as a group of ISGs (195 total) from the Gene Set Enrichment Analysis database, which are listed in Table S4. With this refined list of normalized counts, Z-score values for relative abundance of each heat map were generated by comparing normalized counts from 4 biological replicates each condition that was indicated within that heat map. Morpheus was used to generate the heat maps (https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus). Raw data were deposited with the GEO repository and assigned the accession #GSE331176.

#### LC-MS/MS analysis of CDNs from engineered bacteria

Engineered E. coli were grown as if to prepare for infection, but the final IPTG (1 mM)-inducing back-dilution step contained a 5 mL total culture volume. Bacteria were centrifuged at 1,500xg for 15 min at 4°C. Supernatants were discarded and bacterial pellets were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C until processing. For analyte extraction, pellets were thawed on ice, washed with 400 μL 1xPBS, transferred to Eppendorf tubes, and pelleted by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 10 min at 4°C. Pellets were washed again and pelleted by centrifugation for 20 min at 5,000 rpm at 4°C. Cells were then suspended in 300 μL extraction solvent (2:2:1 CH3N:MeOH:dH2O) and incubated on ice for 15 min with intermittent vortexing followed by for heating for 10 min at 95°C. Samples were centrifuged at max speed for 10 min at 4°C, and supernatant containing cellular extracts were transferred to fresh Eppendorf tubes. Acetonitrile/Methanol extraction was performed two additional times on the remaining pellet but omitting the 95°C heating step. Combined extract supernatants were evaporated using a Speed-Vac for 6–8 hrs at 40°C. Dried samples were sent to Clinical Microbiomics, Inc. where LC-MS/MS was performed to analyze presence of synesthetic cyclic nucleotide products. We included synthetic di- and tri-cyclic nucleotide standards matching the predicted products of the synthetic bacteria based on previous literature49,80,85,87,88,123,124. Initial data analysis was performed by Clinical Microbiomics, Inc to detect the presence of all CDN/CTNs in all synthetic bacterial samples. Data was further analyzed by comparing CDN/CTN signals to control bacteria expressing no cyclase enzyme and imposing a 10-fold cutoff for background subtraction. For samples for which more than one cyclic nucleotide product was predicted, the log-fold enrichment of each CDN was normalized within each individual synthetic bacterial sample to indicate major and minor cyclic nucleotide products.

#### In vivo infections, tumor models, and treatments

CDN desiccates and bacterial pellets (bacteria grown as above) were resuspended in tissue culture 1xPBS, pH 7.4 just prior to injection into mice. Mice were injected intraperitoneally (I.P.) with 400 μg 2′3′-cGA, 400 μg 2′3′-cUA, 880 μg 3′3′-cUA, 1×108 CFU S. epidermidis, 1×108 CFU L. innocua, 1×108 CFU L. lactis, 1×108 CFU L. plantarum, or 1xPBS, pH 7.4 as a control, in 200 μL total volume. 6 hrs after I.P., mice were euthanized and the peritoneum was lavaged with 1 mL of 1xPBS. Peritoneal lavage was centrifuged at 400xg for 10 min at 4°C to pellet cells (for western blot analysis).

B16-OVA cells (see cell culture above) were resuspended in tissue culture 1xPBS, pH 7.4 (3×105 cells) and subcutaneously (S.C.) injected into the lower left belly in 100 μL total volume, or into the upper left back in 200 μL total volume. For I.T. experiments, ClearColi grown as above (with 0.01 mM IPTG present in last 3 hrs of growth) were inactivated by PFA as above. Bacterial pellets were resuspended in tissue culture 1xPBS, pH 7.4 to a concentration of 1×109 CFU/mL. When tumors reached between ~16–64mm2 (approximately 12 days after S.C. injection), mice were stratified via caliper measurements into groups of equal tumor burden and 100 μL (1×108 CFU) was injected I.T., followed by two additional doses that occurred 3 and 7 days later. For intravenous treatments, starting 6 days after S.C. injection of B16-OVA cells, mice underwent four weekly R.O. treatments with 150 μL 1.33×108 CFU/mL bacteria (20×106 CFU). Mice were monitored every 2–3 days for tumor size (via caliper measurements) and euthanized when the humane endpoint was reached, defined as a tumor area > 200 mm2 or tumor ulceration.

For hepatocellular carcinoma models, hepatocytes are transfected in vivo with genetic elements designed to drive tumorigenesis through MYC overexpression and Trp53 loss, via hydrodynamic tail vein injection (HDTVi)75. pT3-EF1a-MYC-IRES-luciferase-OS (MYC-lucOS), px330-sg-p53 (sg-p53), and SB13 transposase-encoding vectors were received as a kind gift from Dr. Amaia Lujambio (Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai) and prepared in large quantities under strict endotoxin free conditions from Genscript. Final plasmids were verified through whole plasmid sequencing and restriction digestion. Tumors were generated as previously described125. Briefly, 12 μg of MYC-lucOS, 12 μg of sg-p53, and 3 μg of SB13 transposase was dissolved in 2 ml of 0.9% NaCl solution (Intermountain) which was injected into the lateral tail vein of mice at a volume corresponding to 10% of their body weight within 5–7 seconds75. For bacterial treatments, mice underwent R.O. treatments with 150 μL 1.33×108 CFU/mL bacteria (20×106 CFU) at the indicated intervals. For R.O. treatment of established tumors, mice were stratified into equal tumor burden prior to treatment via tumor-derived luciferase signal determined through bioluminescent imaging using the IVIS spectrum system (Revvity Health Sciences). IVIS imaging was performed as previously described125. Briefly, mice were injected intraperitoneally with 200 μL 7.5 mg/mL D-luciferin (Revvity Health Sciences) that was resuspended in 1xPBS, pH 7.4 and filtered (0.2 μm, Millipore). Luciferase Signal was quantified using Living Image software (Caliper Life Sciences) and graphed as total flux (p/s) 5 min after injection with D-luciferin. For either B16-OVA or HCC experiments, survival outcomes were determined in a blinded manner.

#### Electrophoretic mobility shift assay

To determine the binding affinity of murine STING with CDNs, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA) were performed following established protocols87. Specifically, 20 nM of α−32P labeled 2′3′-cUA or 3′3′-cUA was incubated with serial dilutions of STING protein ranging from 0.5 nM to 50 μM (concentration of STING dimer) in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 60 mM potassium chloride, 5 mM magnesium chloride, and 1 mM TCEP. Reactions were incubated at room temperature for 10 min and resolved on a 7.2-cm 6% nondenaturing polyacrylamide gel at 100 V for 40 min in 0.5 × Tris-borate (TB) buffer. Following electrophoresis, the gel was fixed in a solution of 40% ethanol and 10% acetic acid for 15 min before drying at 80°C for 40 min. The dried gel was exposed to a phosphor-screen and imaged using a Typhoon Trio Variable Mode Imager (GE Healthcare). Signal intensity was quantified using ImageQuant 5.2 software. Subsequent nonlinear regression (curve fit) analysis and KD calculation were performed with GraphPad Prism (10.3.0) using a one site--specific binding model.

#### X-ray crystallography

Murine Sting gene was synthesized as a gBlock (Integrated DNA Technologies) with ≥18 base pairs of homology flanking the insert sequence and cloned into a custom pETSUMO2 vector by Gibson assembly126. Plasmids were transformed into Top10 competent E. coli. The C-terminal domain of mSTING (N153-E336) was expressed as a recombinant protein as previously described126. Briefly, plasmid was transformed into E. coli strain BL21-RIL (Agilent) and grown as overnight cultures in ~30 mL of MDG media at 37°C with 230 rpm shaking. Overnight cultures were used to inoculate 2 1× liter M9ZB cultures grown at 37°C until OD600 reached 2.5–3.0, then induced with 0.5 mM IPTG and incubated overnight at 16°C with 230 rpm shaking. Bacterial pellets were resuspended and sonicated in lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 400 mM NaCl, 30 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol and 1 mM DTT), clarified by centrifugation at 20,000 rpm (Thermo Fisher Scientific centrifuge with T29–8 × 50 Fixed Angle Rotor) for 30 min at 4°C. Recombinant protein was then purified from the supernatant using 8 mL of packed Ni-NTA resin (Qiagen) in a gravity column and eluted with 20 mL of lysis buffer supplemented to 300 mM imidazole. The eluted protein was dialyzed into 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 250 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT and further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using a 16/600 Superdex 75 column (Cytiva). The SUMO2 tag was removed with recombinant human SENP2 protease (D364–L589, M497A) during dialysis. Protein was concentrated to >10 mg/mL, flash frozen with liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C.

Crystals of the mSTING–2′3′-cUA, mSTING–3′3′-cUA and mSTING–3′3′-cAA complexes were grown at 18°C for 3–10 days using hanging-drop vapor diffusion. Purified mSTING protein was diluted to 5 or 10 mg/mL in a buffer containing 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 75 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT and inculcated with 0.5 or 1 mM of cyclic dinucleotide as indicated. The mixture was incubated at 18°C for 10 min before used to set 4 × 96-well sparse screens with 70 μL for each reservoir solution by mixing 200 nL of protein mixture and 200 nL of reservoir solution for each drop using Mosquito (SPT Labtech). Further optimized crystals were grown in EasyXtal 15-well trays (NeXtal Biotechnologies) with 350 μL reservoir solution and 2 μL drops set with a ratio of 1 μL of protein solution and 1 μL of reservoir solution. Optimized crystallization conditions were as follows: mSTING–2′3′-cUA complex, 0.1M Tris pH 8.5, 30% (w/v) PEG1000; mSTING–3′3′-cUA complex, 0.2M sodium fluoride, 18% (w/v) PEG 3350; mSTING–3′3′-c-di-AMP complex, 200 mM lithium acetate, 20% PEG-3350. Crystals were cryo-protected using reservoir solution supplemented with 10–25% ethylene glycol and harvested with a nylon loop.

X-ray diffraction data for mSTING–2′3′-cUA and mSTING–3′3′-cUA complexes were collected using the automated data collection pipeline at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS2) at Brookhaven National Laboratory with beamline AMX, and data were processed with AutoPROC127. X-ray diffraction data for mSTING–3′3′-cAA were collected with beamline 8.2.1 at the Advanced Light Source (ALS) at Lawrence Berkey National Laboratory, and data were processed with XDS (https://doi.org/10.1107/S0907444909047337) and Aimless (https://doi.org/10.1107/S0907444913000061). The structure of mSTING–2′3′-cGAMP (PDB: 4LOJ)92 was used for molecular replacement to determine initial phases of all three mSTING-CDN complexes and structural modelling was completed in Coot128. Final structures were refined to stereochemistry statistics with PHENIX129 as reported in Table S6130–132. All structural figures were generated with PyMOL (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, version 2.4.2, Schrödinger, LLC).

### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

All values, unless otherwise indicated, represent the mean ± the standard error of the mean (SEM) of at least 3 independent replicates. Heat map values represent the mean of at least n = 3 biological replicates. All shown immunoblots and micrographs are representative of at least n = 3 biological replicates. Unless otherwise indicated, a two tailed student’s t-test was performed to determine significance, which was defined as a *p-value less than 0.05. For in vivo experiments, p-values were further demarcated as ** < 0.01, *** < 0.001, and **** < 0.0001. To determine significance for survival studies, a Logrank (Mantel-cox) test was used. A Mann-Whitney test was performed to determine significance for IVIS values.
